fixes.explanation: Yes. Joseph speaks to Pharaoh's court and asks them to pass his words to Pharaoh, Egypt's king (Genesis 50:4). In his message he says his father made him swear an oath when he said, “I am about to die. You must bury me in the tomb that I dug for myself in the land of Canaan.” (Genesis 50:5). So the oath is about Canaan, and about a tomb Jacob says he dug himself.

That's the order, baker. Joseph, Jacob's son, directs the physicians in his service to embalm his father Israel, and they do it (Genesis 50:2). He gives the job to the people who work for him. The next verse says the embalming takes forty days to complete (Genesis 50:3). I think that tells us how carefully Joseph wanted his father looked after.

Yes, and it's loud. At the threshing floor of Atad, “…they lamented and wailed loudly, and Joseph mourned for his father seven days.” (Genesis 50:10). That's grief you can hear from a distance. The next verse says the Canaanites living there see the mourning (Genesis 50:11).

The Amorites aren't the ones the Canaanites name, baker. They see the mourning at Atad and say, “This is a solemn ceremony of mourning by the Egyptians.” (Genesis 50:11). And the text says that's how the place across the Jordan came to be called Abel-mizraim. With Egyptian elders and chariots in that crowd, I can see why they said it.

Leaving isn't what he says, friend. The brothers come bowing low, scared that Joseph might repay them, and his first words are, “Do not be afraid.” (Genesis 50:19). Then he tells them, “I will provide for you and your little ones.” (Genesis 50:21). I think that's the point: a man who promises to feed your little ones isn't sending you away. He's keeping you close, and the text says he spoke kindly to them.
